llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan  
“Funding requirements, financing constraints, and corporate investment”

====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD) implemented in a Difference-in-Differences (RD-in-Time) framework.

Why RD?  
• U.S. pension law (ERISA + PPA predecessors) imposes sharply higher minimum contributions once the plan’s funding ratio (assets ÷ projected benefit obligation) falls below a statutory threshold (e.g., 90 %).  
• Firms just below the cutoff face a large, plausibly exogenous jump in required cash outflows; firms just above do not.  
• Near the cutoff, assignment to “high-contribution” status is as-good-as random except for the forcing variable (funding ratio).  

Why “fuzzy”?  
• Some firms below the threshold receive temporary waivers or choose to contribute more than required; likewise, some slightly above contribute voluntarily. Hence the jump in contributions is large but not deterministic.  

Why add a DiD/time dimension?  
• The threshold is re-evaluated each year. We can difference out firm fixed effects and common macro shocks, reducing bias from unobserved heterogeneity and time trends in investment.  

Econometric form:  
Invest_it = α + τ · PostBelow_it + f(FundingRatio_it) + γ_i + δ_t + ε_it  
where PostBelow_it = 1 if firm i is below the threshold in year t (treatment),  
f(·) is a flexible polynomial or local linear control for the running variable, γ_i are firm FE, δ_t year FE.  
τ is interpreted as the local average treatment effect (LATE) of binding funding requirements on investment for firms at the cutoff.

====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Running (forcing) variable: FundingRatio_it = PlanAssets / PBO, expressed in %.  

Cutoff: 0.90 (or the exact statutory level in sample years).  

Treatment indicator (Z_it): Below_it = 1{FundingRatio_it < 0.90}.  

First-stage (dose): Actual pension contribution scaled by assets or sales (Contrib_it).  

Reduced-form outcome: Corporate investment (Capex_it / PPE_{t-1} or Capex / Assets).  

Treatment (complier) group: Firms whose funding ratios place them just below the threshold and whose contributions respond sharply (local bandwidth h).  

Control group: Firms just above the threshold within the same bandwidth.  

Timing: Annual; treatment resets each year conditional on the current funding ratio.

====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Local continuity: In the absence of the regulation, expected investment would vary smoothly with the funding ratio at the cutoff.  
— Plausible: the ratio is an accounting object influenced by market returns and actuarial assumptions, not directly by investment opportunities.

A2. No precise manipulation of FundingRatio around 0.90.  
— Reasonable: Funding ratios depend on market returns and actuarial valuations that managers cannot perfectly fine-tune at year-end. We will test this (McCrary density test).

A3. Exclusion / monotonicity in FRD: Crossing the threshold affects investment only through the regulatory increase in pension contributions (no other discrete regulatory changes at exactly 0.90).  
— Supported by pension law; we will show no other discontinuities in tax, accounting, or governance rules at that level.

A4. Stable unit treatment: One firm’s status does not affect another’s investment (plausible).

====================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation / smoothing of the funding ratio.  
  • Test density of FundingRatio around cutoff (McCrary).  
  • Compare actuarial assumption choices (discount rate, wage growth) above vs. below cutoff.  
  • Show no jump in firm characteristics unrelated to pensions (size, leverage).

T2. Concurrent shocks correlated with underfunding (e.g., negative stock returns) could lower both FundingRatio and investment.  
  • RD controls for the continuous realization of FundingRatio; only the discrete jump drives identification.  
  • Include firm×industry trends and market return controls.  
  • Show smoothness in Tobin’s q, cash flow at cutoff.

T3. Heterogeneous investment opportunities (e.g., distressed firms).  
  • Add controls for ROA, sales growth; allow different slopes on each side of cutoff.  
  • Conduct placebo RD at alternative pseudo-cutoffs (e.g., 80 %, 100 %) to show no effect where regulation is absent.

====================================================================
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast high-dimensional FE
library(rdrobust)     # RD estimation
library(rddensity)    # McCrary test

# 1. Load data
df <- read_csv("firm_pension_investment.csv")   # one row per firm-year

# 2. Variable construction
df <- df %>%
  mutate(funding_ratio = plan_assets / pbo,
         distance     = funding_ratio - 0.90,           # running variable distance
         below        = if_else(funding_ratio < 0.90, 1, 0),
         contrib_rate = pension_contrib / lag(total_assets),
         invest_rate  = capex / lag(ppent),             # main outcome
         abs_distance = abs(distance))

# 3. Choose a bandwidth (e.g., ±7.5 pct-points)
bw <- 0.075
rd_sample <- df %>% filter(abs_distance <= bw, !is.na(invest_rate), !is.na(contrib_rate))

# 4. First-stage: does below threshold raise contributions?
feols(contrib_rate ~ below + distance + i(distance, 2) | firm_id + year, data = rd_sample)

# 5. Reduced form (intention-to-treat)
feols(invest_rate ~ below + distance + i(distance, 2) | firm_id + year, data = rd_sample)

# 6. Fuzzy RD with rdrobust (local linear, bias-corrected)
rd_res <- rdrobust(y = rd_sample$invest_rate,
                   x = rd_sample$distance,
                   fuzzy = rd_sample$below,
                   bwselect = "mserd")       # automatic bandwidth
summary(rd_res)

# 7. Robustness: Density test for manipulation
rddensity(rd_sample$distance)$summary

# 8. Placebo cutoff at 1.05
placebo <- rdrobust(y = rd_sample$invest_rate,
                    x = rd_sample$funding_ratio - 1.05)
summary(placebo)
```

====================================================================
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory: Binding pension contributions drain internal liquidity, forcing financially constrained firms to scale back investment.  

Sign (+/–): Negative.  

Magnitude (order-of-magnitude prior): For firms at the cutoff, a 1 ppt increase in required contributions (≈0.3 % of assets) may reduce investment by 0.6–1.0 ppt of PPE (roughly 5–10 % of the mean investment rate). This aligns with standard elasticities in the financing-constraint literature.

====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = doubtful)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. No manipulation of running variable .............. 0.8  
2. Local continuity of potential outcomes ........... 0.8  
3. Strong first stage (jump in contributions) ....... 1.0  
4. No other policy discontinuity at cutoff .......... 0.7  
5. SUTVA / no spillovers ............................ 0.9  

Overall internal validity: Good but not perfect; primary concern is possible endogenous actuarial assumptions around the cutoff, which we partially mitigate with tests and robustness checks.

====================================================================
This plan delivers a transparent, plausibly causal estimate of how exogenous liquidity shocks—imposed by pension-funding regulation—affect corporate investment behavior.
